summary: This standards-track memo defines the MIB objects for managing UDP implementations through SNMP, independent of IP version. It obsoletes earlier UDP MIB definitions.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP is the protocol a network manager uses to ask a device about itself. This document defines the questions to ask about UDP: how many datagrams came in and went out, how many arrived with nobody listening, and what every open UDP socket on the machine is. The table of sockets works for both IPv4 and IPv6, and it can also describe a socket that only talks to one particular remote host.

questions: how to monitor udp with snmp
how to list udp endpoints with snmp
what replaced the ipv6 udp mib
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router exposes so a manager can count UDP traffic and list every UDP endpoint it holds.

tldr.problem: A network manager needs to know how much UDP traffic a host is carrying and which UDP sockets are open, but the original SNMP objects for UDP only described IPv4 and could not describe a socket bound to one remote address.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module with one table, the udpEndpointTable, whose rows are indexed by the local and remote address type, address and port, and a group of counters such as udpInDatagrams and udpHCOutDatagrams.
tldr.outcome: One table now covers both IP versions and both listening and connected endpoints, and it reports which operating system process owns each endpoint. The module obsoletes RFC 2013 and RFC 2454, whose IPv6 table has been moved to Historic.

facts.label: High-capacity counters
facts.value: For more than 1 million datagrams per second

facts.label: Address octet limit
facts.value: 111 octets for the local and remote addresses together

today: RFC 4113 is a Proposed Standard from June 2005 and has not been obsoleted. It replaced the IPv4-only RFC 2013 and the separate IPv6 table of RFC 2454 with a single table that covers both IP versions, and the IPV6-UDP-MIB it replaced has been moved to Historic.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), and they are generally accessed with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The objects are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant with SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The wider management framework is described in Section 7 of RFC 3410.

For a reader who has never used SNMP: a managed object is a named value that a device exposes, such as a counter of packets sent. The MIB is the catalogue that gives those values names and types. A manager reads them over SNMP by walking the catalogue, and SNMPv3 adds authentication and privacy to that exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: A managed object is a named value that a device exposes, such as a counter of packets sent. The MIB is the catalogue that gives those values names and types, and a manager reads them over SNMP by walking that catalogue.

sections.title: Overview: The UDP MIB
sections.content:
The memo defines the part of the MIB that describes implementations of the User Datagram Protocol, as defined in RFC 768, in an IP version independent manner. The module consists of one table and a group of scalars.

The udp group of scalars reports parameters and statistics of a UDP protocol engine. Two of them, udpHCInDatagrams and udpHCOutDatagrams, were added after RFC 2013 to provide high-capacity counters for fast networks. Discontinuities in the values of the counters in this group are indicated by discontinuities in the value of the sysUpTime object, which is defined in RFC 3418.

The udpEndpointTable gives access to status information for all the UDP endpoints a UDP protocol engine handles. It covers strictly listening endpoints, as the historical udpTable did, and also connected endpoints, which accept packets only from a given remote system. It also reports which operating system level process handles each UDP connection. Addresses and ports in the table use the InetAddressType, InetAddress and InetPortNumber textual conventions defined in RFC 4001.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has two parts. A group of counters says how much UDP traffic the device handled. A table lists every UDP endpoint it holds, whether the endpoint is listening for anyone or bound to one particular remote host, and which program on the machine is using it.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
UDP related objects were originally part of the RFC1213-MIB, defined in RFC 1213, and were later copied into a separate module and published in SMIv2 form as RFC 2013. Both earlier versions of the UDP-MIB defined the udpTable, which is deprecated for two reasons.

The first is that the udpTable supports IPv4 only. The approach in the IETF is to write IP version neutral MIBs rather than separate definitions for each version of IP, so that new objects are added in one place; the approach of RFC 2454 with separate tables is therefore not continued. The second is that the udpTable cannot describe connected UDP endpoints. Connected endpoints behave differently from listening ones and are managed differently, so adding the remote endpoint information to the udpEndpointTable leaves room for status and statistic objects specific to them.

The IPV6-UDP-MIB of RFC 2454 has been moved to Historic, because the approach of separate IP version specific tables is no longer followed, and implementing RFC 2454 is no longer suggested. Because scoped addresses are now represented with the IPv4z and IPv6z address types, there is no longer a need to include the interface index in the index of the udpEndpointTable, which is a change from the use of ipv6UdpIfIndex in RFC 2454.

The table reports the identification of the operating system level process that handles a connection or a listening endpoint, as an Unsigned32 value. It is expected to be the same as the hrSWRunIndex of the HOST-RESOURCES-MIB in RFC 2790, if the value is smaller than 2147483647, or the sysApplElmtRunIndex of the SYSAPPL-MIB in RFC 2287. This lets a management application identify the UDP connections that belong to a particular program, which has proved valuable in operational environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The old table only understood IPv4 and could not describe a socket that talks to one fixed remote host, so it is deprecated. This document replaces it with one table that works for both IP versions, and it also links each endpoint to the program on the machine that owns it, using the identifiers that other management modules already use.

sections.title: The Managed Objects
sections.content:
The scalars of the udp group are counters, all with read-only access: udpInDatagrams at { udp 1 } counts the datagrams delivered to UDP users, udpNoPorts at { udp 2 } counts the received datagrams for which there was no application at the destination port, udpInErrors at { udp 3 } counts the received datagrams that could not be delivered for reasons other than that, and udpOutDatagrams at { udp 4 } counts the datagrams sent from the entity. The two high-capacity counters, udpHCInDatagrams at { udp 8 } and udpHCOutDatagrams at { udp 9 }, are 64-bit counters for devices that can receive or transmit more than 1 million UDP datagrams per second. Discontinuities in any of these counters can occur when the management system is re-initialised, and at other times indicated by discontinuities in sysUpTime.

The udpEndpointTable, at { udp 7 }, holds one row per current UDP endpoint, and a row is identified by seven index columns: udpEndpointLocalAddressType, udpEndpointLocalAddress, udpEndpointLocalPort, udpEndpointRemoteAddressType, udpEndpointRemoteAddress, udpEndpointRemotePort and udpEndpointInstance. The address type in the table is the address type used for the communication, whatever higher-level abstraction the application uses, so an application that uses IPv6 sockets to talk IPv4 between ::ffff:10.0.0.1 and ::ffff:10.0.0.2 still uses unknown(0) value ipv4(1) for the address type. The instance column, whose range starts at 1, distinguishes several processes connected to the same endpoint, which on a system using BSD sockets is what supports the SO_REUSEADDR and SO_REUSEPORT options. The only readable column of the table is udpEndpointProcess, which holds the process identifier of the program associated with the endpoint, or zero when there is no such process.

Implementers are warned about the length of the key. If the total number of elements in udpEndpointLocalAddress and udpEndpointRemoteAddress exceeds 111, the object identifiers of the column instances have more than 128 sub-identifiers and cannot be accessed with SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3, so the table should not hold entries that would produce such identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters are simple totals: datagrams in, datagrams out, datagrams that arrived with nobody listening, and datagrams that could not be handed over. The table is keyed by the local and remote address and port, so each row is one open socket, and the last readable value in the row is the identifier of the program that owns it.

sections.title: How a Listening Application Appears
sections.content:
Because the table can describe a socket bound to a remote host, the document sets out how a listening application is represented, in three ways.

  • An application willing to accept both IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams is represented by a udpEndpointLocalAddressType of unknown(0) and a udpEndpointLocalAddress of a zero-length octet string.
  • An application willing to accept only IPv4 or only IPv6 is represented by the appropriate address type and a udpEndpointLocalAddress of '0.0.0.0' or '::' respectively.
  • An application listening for datagrams only for one specific IP address, but from any remote system, is represented by the appropriate address type with udpEndpointLocalAddress set to that local address.

In every case where the remote side is a wildcard, udpEndpointRemoteAddressType is unknown(0), udpEndpointRemoteAddress is a zero-length octet string, and udpEndpointRemotePort is 0. If the operating system demultiplexes UDP packets by remote address and port, or the application has connected its socket by specifying a default remote address and port, the remote values should be filled in to reflect that.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket that accepts traffic from anyone is recorded with an empty remote address and port zero. A socket that talks to one fixed host is recorded with that host's address and port. A socket that accepts both IPv4 and IPv6 is recorded with a special address type and an empty local address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a read-write or read-create access clause, so if the module is implemented correctly there is no risk that an intruder can alter or create objects of this module with a direct SNMP SET operation.

Some of the readable objects may still be sensitive in some environments, and even reading them should be controlled. The indices of the udpEndpointTable and the udpTable contain information about the listeners on an entity: the udpEndpointLocalPort and udpLocalPort objects in the indices reveal which ports are open on the machine and therefore which attacks are likely to succeed, without the attacker having to run a port scanner.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change the objects of this module. The document recommends that implementors use the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is then the operator's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that only principals with legitimate rights can reach these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in this module is read-only, so nobody can change a value through it. Reading is a different matter: the table shows which ports are open, which is a map of the machine for anyone who should not have it. The document therefore asks for SNMPv3 with encryption and authentication, and for access to be limited to the accounts that need it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The MIB module uses the object identifier values recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: the udp group of objects sits at { mib-2 7 } and the udpMIB module at { mib-2 50 }. Within the group, the counters occupy { udp 1 } to { udp 4 }, the deprecated IPv4 udpTable is at { udp 5 }, the current udpEndpointTable is at { udp 7 } and the high-capacity counters are at { udp 8 } and { udp 9 }. The value { udp 6 } was the IPv6 table of the IPV6-UDP-MIB in RFC 2454 and is obsoleted by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The module registers two numbers with IANA: the group of UDP objects and the module itself. The counters and tables inside the group have fixed numbers, so a manager can find them without searching.

viz.caption: THE COLUMNS OF ONE ENDPOINT ROW

items.title: Local address type and address
items.text: The address family and address the endpoint is bound to locally.

items.title: Local port
items.text: The port number the endpoint is bound to.

items.title: Remote address type and address
items.text: The remote family and address, or empty when any remote is accepted.

items.title: Remote port
items.text: The remote port, or zero when any remote is accepted.

items.title: Instance
items.text: Distinguishes several programs connected to the same endpoint.

items.title: Process
items.text: The identifier of the program that owns the endpoint, or zero.
